MND investigations: clinical diagnosis supported by EMG, exclude mimics with imaging; riluzole, NIV, gastrostomy, MDT palliation
Compares respiratory monitoring needs and prognosis; draws structured conclusions
questions.modelAnswer:
These three conditions affect different parts of the motor pathway, and recognising the site of the lesion from the signs drives investigation and treatment.

Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy, often following infection; Campylobacter jejuni is the classic trigger, where molecular mimicry produces antibodies against peripheral nerve gangliosides. Patients develop ascending, broadly symmetrical weakness over days to weeks, with areflexia, distal paraesthesia, back pain and sometimes autonomic instability. Nerve conduction studies show demyelinating or axonal patterns, and CSF classically shows raised protein with a normal cell count. Acute management centres on IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, serial forced vital capacity (peak flow is unreliable), cardiac monitoring, VTE prophylaxis and early critical care referral. Most patients recover substantially.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction, usually caused by antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor, less often to MuSK. Weakness is fatigable and typically affects ocular muscles (ptosis, diplopia) and bulbar and proximal limb muscles, while reflexes and sensation are normal. Investigation includes antibody testing, repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG, and CT of the thorax for thymoma. Treatment combines anticholinesterases for symptoms with immunosuppression and, in selected patients, thymectomy. Myasthenic crisis, with bulbar or respiratory failure, is treated with IVIg or plasma exchange and ventilatory support, and drugs that worsen neuromuscular transmission must be avoided.

Motor neurone disease (MND) is a neurodegenerative disease of upper and lower motor neurones. Its hallmark is a mix of UMN signs (spasticity, brisk reflexes) and LMN signs (wasting, fasciculation) in the same region, with sensation and eye movements spared. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by EMG, with imaging to exclude mimics such as cervical myelopathy. There is no cure. Riluzole modestly prolongs survival, and care focuses on NIV for respiratory failure, gastrostomy, communication aids and advance care planning.

In summary, all three can cause respiratory failure, but GBS and MG are treatable immunological emergencies, while MND needs early palliative planning.

questions.q: Jack, 19, with type 1 diabetes, presents with vomiting and abdominal pain after missing insulin for 2 days. Glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.1 mmol/L, venous pH 7.12, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, sodium 131 mmol/L. He is drowsy but responsive, with deep sighing respiration at 30 a minute, HR 122 and BP 102/64. Describe your management over the first 24 hours, including monitoring and complications.
markScheme: Diagnosis: DKA (meets all three JBDS criteria); pulse >100 is a JBDS severity marker (others include ketones >6, bicarbonate <5, pH <7.0, low admission potassium, GCS <12, anion gap >16)
ABCDE; senior review; consider HDU given severity
IV crystalloid resuscitation, then ongoing replacement per protocol
Fixed-rate IV insulin infusion (weight-based); continue long-acting basal insulin
Potassium: initially high but total-body depleted; add potassium to fluids once below the upper limit and passing urine
Add glucose-containing fluid when glucose <14 mmol/L
Hourly capillary glucose and ketones, venous gas for pH, bicarbonate and potassium at intervals
Resolution: ketones <0.6 mmol/L and pH >7.3; switch to subcutaneous insulin with overlap
Complications: hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema (especially young), VTE, aspiration
Precipitant (missed insulin) and education: sick-day rules, diabetes specialist team review
questions.modelAnswer:
Jack has DKA: ketones 5.1 mmol/L, glucose above 11 mmol/L and pH below 7.3 with bicarbonate below 15 mmol/L. A bicarbonate of 8 mmol/L and pH of 7.12 indicate marked acidosis, and his heart rate above 100 is one of the JBDS markers of severe DKA (others include ketones above 6 mmol/L, bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L, pH below 7.0, hypokalaemia on admission, GCS below 12 and an anion gap above 16), so he needs senior review and consideration of a high-dependency bed. Abdominal pain and vomiting are common in DKA but should settle as acidosis resolves; if not, look for a surgical cause.

After an ABCDE assessment, the first priority is IV crystalloid to restore circulating volume, followed by ongoing replacement according to the hospital DKA protocol, while monitoring fluid balance. A fixed-rate IV insulin infusion based on body weight is started, and his usual long-acting basal insulin is continued so that he is protected when the infusion stops.

Potassium needs careful handling. His serum potassium of 5.6 mmol/L reflects acidosis and insulin deficiency moving potassium out of cells, but total-body potassium is depleted. Once potassium falls into the normal range and he is passing urine, potassium is added to the IV fluids; insulin without replacement can cause dangerous hypokalaemia. When glucose falls below 14 mmol/L, glucose-containing fluid is added so the insulin infusion can continue to clear ketones without causing hypoglycaemia.

Monitoring includes hourly capillary glucose and ketones, and venous gases for pH, bicarbonate and potassium at least at 1, 2 and 4 hours and then regularly, with strict fluid balance and observations. DKA has resolved when ketones are below 0.6 mmol/L and pH is above 7.3. He can then move to subcutaneous insulin once eating, with an overlap before the infusion stops.

Complications to anticipate include hypokalaemia, hypoglycaemia, cerebral oedema (a particular risk in young people with rapid osmotic shifts; watch for headache or falling consciousness), aspiration, VTE and hyperchloraemic acidosis from saline. The diabetes specialist team should review him before discharge, and he needs education on sick-day rules, ketone testing and why he missed insulin.

questions.q: Mr Ahmed, 82, with hypertension and heart failure, is admitted with 4 days of diarrhoea. He takes ramipril, furosemide, spironolactone and ibuprofen for knee pain. Creatinine is 245 µmol/L (baseline 98), potassium 6.3 mmol/L, BP 96/60, ECG shows peaked T waves only. He looks dry, his JVP is not visible and his urine output has been low for a day. Explain the likely causes and outline management.
markScheme: Creatinine 2.5 × baseline: KDIGO stage 2 AKI
Pre-renal AKI from volume depletion due to diarrhoea
Compounded by drugs: ACE inhibitor (efferent dilatation), NSAID (afferent constriction), diuretics
Hyperkalaemia from AKI plus ACE inhibitor and spironolactone; moderate grade with ECG change
Stop ramipril, spironolactone, ibuprofen; withhold furosemide
Cautious IV fluid resuscitation, balancing his heart failure; regular review and fluid balance
Hyperkalaemia: IV calcium because of ECG changes, insulin–glucose, consider salbutamol; binder
Monitor potassium, creatinine, urine output, cardiac monitoring
Stool cultures/C. difficile, urine dip, ultrasound if not improving
On recovery: careful reintroduction of heart failure drugs; stop NSAID long term; sick-day guidance
questions.modelAnswer:
His creatinine is 245 ÷ 98 ≈ 2.5 times baseline, which is KDIGO stage 2 acute kidney injury. The most likely cause is pre-renal: four days of diarrhoea have reduced his circulating volume, and he is hypotensive at 96/60.

His medications have worsened the injury. Glomerular filtration in hypovolaemia depends on prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar dilatation and angiotensin II-mediated efferent constriction. Ibuprofen blocks the first and ramipril blocks the second, while furosemide and spironolactone add volume depletion. This combination is sometimes called the "triple whammy". Hyperkalaemia of 6.3 mmol/L (moderate) results from reduced potassium excretion, made worse by the ACE inhibitor and the mineralocorticoid antagonist.

Because there are ECG changes, he should receive IV calcium to stabilise the myocardium, followed by insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells, with nebulised salbutamol as an adjunct if tolerated given his heart disease. A potassium binder can help remove potassium. He needs cardiac monitoring and repeat potassium measurements, and capillary glucose monitoring after insulin.

Ramipril, spironolactone and ibuprofen should be stopped, and furosemide withheld. Fluid resuscitation should be careful and repeatedly reassessed, as his heart failure makes him vulnerable to pulmonary oedema; fluid balance and daily weights are essential. Send stool cultures including C. difficile, dipstick the urine, and request a renal ultrasound if he does not improve or obstruction is possible. Persistent refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis or fluid overload would prompt renal referral for replacement therapy.

On recovery, his heart failure drugs should be reintroduced one at a time with monitoring of renal function and potassium, because they improve his prognosis. Ibuprofen should be stopped permanently and alternative analgesia offered. He should be given sick-day guidance to pause these drugs temporarily during dehydrating illness.

questions.q: Essay: "Chronic kidney disease is better understood as a cardiovascular risk state than as a pathway to dialysis." Critically evaluate this proposition with reference to classification, complications and current management of CKD.
markScheme: Defines CKD and G/A classification; notes most patients never reach kidney failure
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in CKD; risk rises with lower eGFR and higher ACR
Mechanisms: hypertension, vascular calcification (CKD-MBD), inflammation, anaemia, LVH
Albuminuria as marker of both renal and cardiovascular risk
Management targets both: BP control, RAS blockade, statins (cardiovascular protection)
SGLT2 inhibitors protect kidneys and heart (e.g. DAPA-CKD 2020, EMPA-KIDNEY 2023)
Kidney failure risk prediction (KFRE) identifies the minority needing RRT planning
Counterpoint: kidney-specific issues (anaemia, bone disease, acidosis, dialysis planning, transplant, glomerular disease) matter
Equity and patient-centred considerations (frail elderly, conservative care)
Balanced conclusion: dual framing, risk-stratified
questions.modelAnswer:
CKD is defined as abnormal kidney structure or function lasting more than three months. It is classified by eGFR category (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3), a two-dimensional system that reflects the fact that both reduced filtration and albumin leakage independently predict outcomes.

The proposition has strong support. Most people with CKD, particularly the large population with G3a disease and little albuminuria, will never need dialysis; they are far more likely to die from cardiovascular disease. Cardiovascular risk rises steadily as eGFR falls and ACR rises. The mechanisms include hypertension, accelerated atherosclerosis, vascular calcification driven by CKD–mineral and bone disorder, chronic inflammation, anaemia and left ventricular hypertrophy. Albuminuria is a marker of systemic endothelial damage as well as glomerular injury.

Current management reflects this dual risk. Blood-pressure control and renin–angiotensin blockade in albuminuric patients slow progression and protect the heart. Statins are recommended for cardiovascular prevention in CKD, though they do not slow kidney decline. SGLT2 inhibitors best demonstrate the overlap: DAPA-CKD (2020) and EMPA-KIDNEY (2023) showed reductions in kidney disease progression and cardiovascular events, with benefits extending beyond diabetes. The kidney failure risk equation (KFRE), now used in NICE NG203 referral criteria, deliberately identifies the minority whose risk of reaching kidney failure warrants specialist planning.

However, framing CKD only as a cardiovascular risk state is too narrow. Specific kidney complications, such as renal anaemia, bone disease, acidosis, hyperkalaemia and drug dosing, need targeted management. Some patients have treatable glomerulonephritis or genetic disease that requires a specific diagnosis. For those who do progress, timely preparation for dialysis access, pre-emptive transplantation or conservative kidney management determines quality of life. In frail older people, a purely cardiovascular focus may lead to overtreatment.

In conclusion, the proposition is broadly correct for most patients, and it usefully redirects attention to cardiovascular prevention. The best model is risk-stratified: treat cardiovascular risk in everyone with CKD, and use eGFR, ACR and KFRE to identify the minority who need kidney-specific and replacement planning.

questions.q: Mrs Clarke, 67, two days after a laparotomy, is found confused. RR 28, SpO₂ 91% on air, BP 84/46, HR 126, temperature 38.9 °C, new confusion. Her abdomen is distended and tender with guarding, and lactate is 4.6 mmol/L. The operation was an anterior resection for rectal cancer, and she had been progressing well until this morning. Her urine output has been under 20 mL an hour for 4 hours. Calculate her NEWS2, explain the diagnosis using current definitions, and describe your management, including when to escalate.
markScheme: NEWS2: RR 3, SpO₂ 3, air 0, SBP 3, HR 2, new confusion 3, temp 1 = 15 → emergency response
Suspected sepsis with organ dysfunction (hypotension, confusion, hypoxia, high lactate), Sepsis-3
Likely abdominal source, e.g. anastomotic leak or collection
Septic shock if hypotension persists needing vasopressors with lactate >2 after adequate fluid
ABCDE with high-flow oxygen to target 94–98%
Sepsis Six: cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, fluids, lactate, urine output
IV fluid boluses with reassessment; catheter and hourly urine output
Urgent critical care review for vasopressors and invasive monitoring
Urgent surgical review; CT abdomen/pelvis once stabilised; source control (relaparotomy/drainage)
Communication, escalation, documentation and early discussion with family; treatment escalation plan
questions.modelAnswer:
Her NEWS2 is: respiratory rate 28 (3), SpO₂ 91% on air (3), no supplemental oxygen (0), systolic BP 84 (3), pulse 126 (2), new confusion (3) and temperature 38.9 °C (1), giving a total of 15. This is far above the emergency threshold of 7 and needs an immediate senior response.

Under Sepsis-3, sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. She has evidence of infection (fever, peritonism after bowel surgery) and multiple organ dysfunction: hypotension, confusion, hypoxaemia and a lactate of 4.6 mmol/L. If she still needs vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg with lactate above 2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitation, she meets the definition of septic shock. The most likely source is intra-abdominal, such as an anastomotic leak or collection, though pneumonia and line infection should also be considered.

Management begins with an ABCDE assessment and high-flow oxygen titrated to 94–98%. The Sepsis Six are delivered immediately: blood cultures (plus other relevant cultures), broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering bowel flora according to local policy within one hour, IV fluid boluses with reassessment after each, serial lactate, and catheterisation with hourly urine output. Bloods include FBC, renal and liver function, clotting, group and save and a gas.

Escalation is urgent and parallel, not sequential. Critical care should review her immediately, as persistent hypotension needs vasopressors, arterial and central access, and possibly organ support. The surgical team must be told at once, because antibiotics alone will not control a leak; once she is stable enough, CT abdomen and pelvis should define the source, followed by relaparotomy or radiological drainage. A treatment escalation plan should be agreed with senior clinicians and, where possible, with Mrs Clarke and her family, and every step should be documented with timings.

The key messages are recognition through NEWS2, time-critical antibiotics, and source control.
